Illustration: Federico Yankelevich/The Guardian Inside Guardian Weekly Germany Not the man for a crisis: inside the 18 September Guardian Weekly Friedrich Merz faces Germany’s biggest test. Plus: AI apocalypse soon? Get the Guardian Weekly delivered to your home address Isobel Montgomery Thu 17 Sep 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 06.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Friedrich Merz is a man with few choices and little popular support as he faces the end of Germany’s postwar settlement and the collapse of all the checks and balances to maintain democratic norms after the second world war and reunification. While Alternative für Deutschland’s success in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt saw the party win 44% of the vote, they are three seats short of a governing majority and, so far, no other party has said they are prepared to work with them, which means that for the moment, at least, the threat of Germany’s first rightwing extremist state government since the Nazi period has not yet come to pass. As Berlin correspondent Deborah Cole explains, Merz is seen as the wrong man to present and sell a political counterpoint to the AfD’s populist policies. Seen as lacking in empathy and political dexterity, his demeanour is in sharp contrast to Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s lead candidate in Saxony-Anhalt. But as Deborah’s Berlin colleague, Kate Connolly , reports, some of Siegmund’s prospective new MPs have questionable backgrounds, including criminal records, Stasi pasts and connections to far-right networks. Clear messaging of simple slogans promising a quick solution to Germany’s economic and social problems are part of the explanation for the AfD’s popularity (there are further state elections coming this weekend) but regular Guardian Europe commentator Carolin Würfel , who grew up in Communist East Germany, suggests that while the politics of grievance may play a part in the electoral success, former West Germany also contributed to why divisions between the two halves of the country persist. Photograph: Posed by model; d3sign/Getty Images The long read has become a regular commute companion. The last one to grab me was about food influencers , their impact on London restaurants and the question of authenticity. The article gets into how that hype is made. Influencers need a steady stream of content to stay relevant, while relying on PR agencies for access. The result is that every meal is incredible and every burger “the best in London”, until none of it means much. Charles Minty, director of commercial strategy, publishing Oasis have just announced yet more comeback gigs to “lift the spirits of the people”/top up their pensions, including a four-night run at Knebworth House in Hertfordshire, the site of two 1996 gigs regarded as era-defining. Richard Nelsson took a fascinating dive into the archive to find out how the Guardian covered those original shows. https://www.politico.eu/article/volodymy.text: U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff will offer Vladimir Putin direct talks with President Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy in an effort to secure a ceasefire. The proposal for three-way leaders’ negotiations on a peace proposal, the first such summit since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022, was announced at a press conference Tuesday after talks in Norway between Zelenskyy and Witkoff. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, who hosted the talks, said Witkoff will travel to Russia Wednesday and set out proposals for peace terms, including the idea of a three-way summit between the leaders. The meeting in Oslo came after days of high tensions between Ukraine and the U.S. president . Advertisement Advertisement “We have hosted today, I would say, good and constructive talks — necessary after events of the last week,” Støre told reporters after the meeting. “Steve Witkoff will fly tomorrow to St. Petersburg where he will be meeting with Russian leadership and exchange ideas from this meeting and the proposals that have been worked on by European and American colleagues, and possibly pave the way for a meeting at leaders’ level.” Previous attempts to get Putin to meet Zelenskyy in person have fallen flat, with the Kremlin recently insisting a meeting could only take place in Moscow . Zelenskyy told the press conference that the day had been positive. He said issues around the future of Ukrainian territory could only be discussed by leaders and that any peace settlement would require genuine security guarantees. A deal would only be acceptable if Ukraine is involved in designing it, he said.
